label: lemma0124
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: onlypossible
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $H$ be an arbitrary rigid $d$-cube in $G$. 
Suppose that $\sigma$ is a singular $(d+1)$-cube, and that the number of $d$-faces supported by $H$ is $>1$. Suppose that
$f_i^a\sigma$ and $f_j^b \sigma$ are two such faces, such that $i<j$. In particular, they are not opposite faces.  We claim that the
only possible $d$-faces that can be supported by $H$ are 
\begin{equation}\label{onlypossible}
f_i^-\sigma, f_i^+\sigma, f_j^-\sigma, f_j^+\sigma.
\end{equation}
We will show that any other face, say $f_k^c\sigma$, $k \ne i,j$, must have a repeated label; in fact we will show that it has a repeated
$(d-2)$-face.
First note that $f_i^a\sigma$ and $f_j^b\sigma$ have a common $(d-1)$-face,
\[
f_i^a f_j^b \sigma = f_{j-1}^b f_i^a \sigma
\]
by the face relations. Rigidity of $H$ implies that the opposite faces in $f_j^b \sigma$ and $f_i^a\sigma$ must also agree, 
so we also have
\[
f_i^{-a}f_j^{b} \sigma = f_{j-1}^{-b} f_i^a \sigma.
\]
There are now several cases, depending on the relative order of $i,j,k$. Consider, for example, $i<k<j$ (the other cases are
similar). Applying $f_{k-1}^c$ to both sides of the last equation gives 
\[
f_{k-1}^c f_i^{-a}f_j^{b} \sigma =f_{k-1}^c f_{j-1}^{-b} f_i^a \sigma,
\]
which reduces by the face relations to
\[
f_{j-2}^{b} f_{i}^{-a} f_k^c \sigma = f_{j-2}^{-b} f_i^{a} f_k^c \sigma.
\]
This shows that $f_k^c \sigma$ has two disjoint $(d-1)$-faces ($f_{i}^{-a} f_k^c \sigma$ and $f_i^{a} f_k^c \sigma$) containing identical
subfaces, and thus $f_k^c \sigma$ is not supported by $H$.

We have shown that only faces listed in (\ref{onlypossible}) can be supported by $H$. An easy argument shows that
if three of them are supported by $H$, then so is the fourth. This completes the proof of Lemma \ref{lemma0124}.

label: chilemma
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{chilemma}
If $H$ is a monophobic $d$-cube in $G$ and $\sigma\in C_{d+1}(G)$ is a singular $(d+1)$-cube,  let ${\mathcal F}(\sigma)$ denote the set of faces of $\sigma$. Define a function $\chi: {\mathcal F}(\sigma) \to \{0, \pm 1\}$ 
by 
\[
\chi(f_i^{\epsilon_i}\sigma) = 
\begin{cases}
0 & \textrm{if $f_i^{\epsilon_i}\sigma$ is not supported by $H$}, \\
\mathrm{sign} (P) & \textrm{if $f_i^{\epsilon_i}\sigma= P\beta_0^H, P \in {\mathcal{H}}_d$}. \\
\end{cases}
\]
Then $\chi(\partial \sigma) = 0$.

title: Definition
body_md:
Suppose that  $F_i^{\epsilon_i}$ and $F_j^{\epsilon_j}$ are adjacent faces of $Q_d$, and let 
$P:  Q_d \to Q_d$ be
the unique reflection of $Q_d$ fixing their intersection. Let $\tilde{P}: Q_{d-1} \to Q_{d-1}$ be the map obtained
by restricting $P$ to  $F_i^{\epsilon_i}$,  with ordering and orientations of axes inherited from $Q_d$.
Then define
\[
\chi(F_i^{\epsilon_i}, F_j^{\epsilon_j}) = \mathrm{sign}(\tilde{P}).
\]
head: environment
name: Sign differences of adjacent faces

label: adjfaces
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{adjfaces}{\rm (Adjacent Faces)}
Let $F_i^{\epsilon_i}$ and $F_j^{\epsilon_j} $ be adjacent faces of $Q_d$ (i.e. $i \ne j$). Then
\[
\mathrm{sign}(F_i^{\epsilon_i}, F_j^{\epsilon_j}) \chi(F_i^{\epsilon_i}, F_j^{\epsilon_j})=-1.
\]
Hence if two adjacent faces of $\sigma$ are supported by $H$, their contributions cancel out in the
computation of $\chi(\partial\sigma)$.
head: environment

label: sgnchi
title: Proof
body_md:
It is immediate that 
$F_i^{\epsilon_i}$ and $F_j^{\epsilon_j} $ are interchanged either by the reflection
$P=P_{ij}$ (if $\epsilon_i =\epsilon_j$) or by the reflection $P=P_iP_j P_{ij}$  (if $\epsilon_i \ne \epsilon_j$).
We know that 
\begin{equation}\label{sgnchi}
\mathrm{sign}(F_i^{\epsilon_i},F_j^{\epsilon_j})= (-1)^{i+j}\epsilon_i \epsilon_j.
\end{equation}
 To compute
$\chi(F_i^{\epsilon_i},F_j^{\epsilon_j})$ we must identify $\tilde{P}$ and compute its sign. 

Without loss of generality, assume that $i<j$.
We may construct $\tilde{P}$ from $P$ as follows: 
first write $P$ as a signed permutation, then drop $i$ (or $\bar{i}$), as appropriate, and finally, reduce 
all occurrences of $j$ (or $\bar{j}$) by one if $j>i$.

For example, if $n=3$ and $P: F_1^+\longleftrightarrow F_3^-$ (as illustrated above) then $P = P_1P_3 P_{13}$, and
we get 
\[
P = \bar{3}2\bar{1}  \longrightarrow  \bar{3} 2 \longrightarrow  \bar{2} 1 = \tilde{P}
\]
It is clear from this construction that $(-1)^{\mathrm{INV}}(\tilde{P})= (-1)^{j-i-1}$ and 
${\mathrm{FLIP}}(\tilde{P}) = 0$ or $1$ according to whether $\epsilon_i = \epsilon_j$ or $ \epsilon_i = -\epsilon_j$. Hence
\[
\chi(F_i^{\epsilon_i},F_j^{\epsilon_j} )= \mathrm{sign}(\tilde{P}) = 
\begin{cases}
(-1)^{j-i-1} & \textrm{if } \epsilon_i = \epsilon_j \\
(-1)^{j-i} & \textrm{if } \epsilon_i = - \epsilon_j \\
\end{cases}
\]
which can be rewritten as 
\begin{equation}\label{sgnchi2}
\chi(F_i^{\epsilon_i},F_j^{\epsilon_j} )= (-1)^{j-i-1} \epsilon_i \epsilon_j. 
\end{equation}
Combining (\ref{sgnchi}) with (\ref{sgnchi2}) proves Lemma \ref{adjfaces}

label: pert
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{pert}
Let $T: Q^0_d\to Q^0_d$ be a bijective graph map such that 
$d(v,Tv) \le 1$ for all vertices $v\in Q^0_d$, where $d$ denotes Hamming distance.  Then $T$ is either the identity,  a quarter turn $P_i P_{ij}$ 
involving two axis directions, or an axis reflection $P_i$ across a hyperplane separating a face from its opposite.

label: oppfaces
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{oppfaces}{\rm (Cancellation Across Opposite Faces).}
Let $\sigma$ be a nondegenerate singular $d+1$ cube with exactly two faces  supported by a $d$-cube $H$ in $G$, and suppose that these faces are opposite, say $f_k^-\sigma$ and $f_k^+\sigma$. Then $f_k^+\sigma$ is obtained from 
$f_k^-\sigma$ by a rotation of its domain by an element of  ${\mathcal{H}}_d$, specifically, a quarter-turn  $P_i P_{ij}$ through one of its $2$-dimensional faces. 
Hence the contributions of $f_k^-\sigma$ and $f_k^+\sigma$ cancel out in the
computation of $\chi(\partial\sigma)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Faces  $f_k^-\sigma$ and $f_k^+\sigma$ define a bijective graph map $T: Q^0_d\to Q^0_d$ satisfying the conditions
of Proposition \ref{pert}.  Clearly $T$ is not the identity, since $\sigma$ is not degenerate. Hence by Proposition \ref{pert}, either
$T = P_i P_{ij}$ or $T = P_i$, for some $i,j$. An easy argument shows that in the latter case there are four faces supported by $H$, 
not two as was assumed. Hence $T = P_i P_{ij}$ and since $\chi(f_k^-\sigma) = \chi(f_k^+\sigma) = +1$, the contributions of these
faces cancel out in the computation of $\chi(\partial\sigma)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma \ref{lemma0124}, if $\sigma$ has any faces supported by $H$, then there are just three possible cases: 
\begin{enumerate}
\item [(1)]
a single adjacent pair, $f_i^{\epsilon_i} \sigma, f_j^{\epsilon_j} \sigma$, $i\ne j$,
\item[(2)]
a $4$-cycle of faces, each adjacent to the next,
\item[(3)]
a single opposite pair,
$f_i^{- }\sigma, f_i^{+} \sigma$.
\end{enumerate}
Applying $\chi$ to $\partial \sigma$ leaves either $2$ or $4$ nonzero terms, according to these cases.  Lemma \ref{adjfaces} shows that these terms cancel in cases (1) and (2). Lemma \ref{oppfaces} shows that they cancel in case (3). This completes the proof of Lemma \ref{chilemma}. \qed
head: manual
name: Lemma \refchilemma

title: Proof
body_md:
The first statement is an immediate consequence of Lemma \ref{chilemma}. 
To prove the second statement, suppose that
$\alpha: (I_\infty^d, \partial I_\infty^d) \to (G,v_0)$, and 
$h:I_\infty^d \times I_m \to G$ is a homotopy of length $m$ from $\alpha$ to the zero map. If we count 
(with multiplicity) the number of occurrences of $d$-cubes supported by $H$ as faces of $(d+1)$-cubes
in $\alpha(I_\infty^d \times I_m)$, this number is odd:  it is odd on the top layer $ I_\infty^d \times \{0\}$, even on the bottom layer $ I_\infty^d \times \{m\}$, and 
occurrences in the middle layers come in pairs. However, by hypothesis and Lemma \ref{lemma0124}, the number on each $(d+1)$-cube is even. 
This is a contradiction. \qed

label: suffcondition
title: Theorem
body_md:
{\rm (Sufficient Condition for Monophobicity)}\label{suffcondition}
Let  $H$ be a rigid $d$-cube in $G$, with $d \ge 2$.  If $N_G(H)$ contains no subgraphs isomorphic to $K_{23}$, then 
$H$ is monophobic in $G$ if for every $h_0\in H$, either
\begin{enumerate}
\item   forcing  is satisfied at $h_0$, or
\item 
 forcing  fails at $h_0$, but 
 for every $p\in N_G(h_0)-H$ there exists a pair of neighbors $h_1, h_2$ of $h_0$ such that for every $x_1,x_2$ 
with 
paths $p \simeq x_{1}\simeq h_1$ and  $p \simeq x_{2}\simeq h_2$, $x_{1},x_{2}\ne h_0$, the set
$\{x_{1},x_{ 2}, h_{12}\}$ has no common neighbor.
(Here $h_{12}$ denotes the fourth element of the 2-face of $H$ containing $h_0, h_1$, and $h_2$,
and $\simeq$ means that elements in the path may repeat.) 
\end{enumerate}
If $d\le2$, the conditions of this theorem are both necessary and sufficient; if $d>2$ they are sufficient.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
{\rm (Sketch)}
The proof of Theorem \ref{gridlemma} assumes that $N_G(H)$ embeds in a grid neighborhood of $H$. However, a close reading of that proof  shows that only the hypotheses of  Theorem \ref{suffcondition} 
 are used. In fact, forcing always holds at every vertex of  $H$ in a grid neighborhood, and so only condition (1) is used in that case.

If $d=1$, monophobicity is equivalent to avoiding triangles and the result is elementary, so we may
assume that $d\ge 2$. Proceeding as in the proof of Theorem \ref{gridlemma}, we suppose that $\sigma $ is a singular $(d+1)$-cube with $f_{d+1}^-\sigma$ supported by $H$. 
Assuming the conditions of Theorem \ref{suffcondition}, the goal is to show that at least one more face is supported by $H$.  If 
not, there must be a vertex
$h_0\in H$ not appearing in $f_{d+1}^+\sigma$, and we may assume without loss of generality that $\sigma(\vec{0}) = h_0$. 

The first step will be to show that $\sigma(\vec{e}_{d+1}) = h_k$ for some $h_k$ adjacent to $h_0$. Suppose, otherwise,
that $\sigma(\vec{e}_{d+1}) = p$  for some $p \not\in H$.
If condition (1) holds at $h_0$, then
we have a contradiction, since then  $h_0$ is forced to appear in $f_{d+1}^+\sigma$.
If condition (1) fails at $h_0\in H$, then for every $h_k$, $1 \le k \le d$ there is a path 
$p \simeq x_{k} \simeq h_k$ with $x_{k} \ne h_0$. Condition (2) now yields a contradiction, since $\sigma$
must contain a 3-face with vertices labeled as above. Thus we conclude that $\sigma(\vec{e}_{d+1}) = h_k$ for some $h_k$.

Subsequent steps use only the fact that $N_G(H)$ contains no copies of $K_{23}$, and involve  2-faces of $f_{k}^-\sigma$ of the form
  \begin{center}
     \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=1.5]
\tikzset{VertexStyle/.style = {shape= circle,
ball color = gray,text= black,inner sep= 0pt,outer sep= 0pt,minimum size= 5pt}} 
   \Vertex[LabelOut,Lpos=225,x=0 ,y=0,L=${\color{blue}h_S}$]{1}
     \Vertex[LabelOut,Lpos=325,x=1 ,y=0,L=${\color{blue}h_{Sk}}$]{2}
       \Vertex[LabelOut,Lpos=180,x=0 ,y=1,L=${\color{blue}h_{S(d+1)}}$]{3}
         \Vertex[LabelOut,Lpos=0,x=1 ,y=1,L=${\color{blue}X}$]{4}                   
    \Edge[style={thick},color=black](1)(2)
      \Edge[style={thick},color=black](3)(4)
        \Edge[style={thick},color=black](1)(3)
          \Edge[style={thick},color=black](2)(4)      
          \end{tikzpicture} 
    \end{center}
where three of the values (vertices in $H$) are known and the fourth remains to be determined. Since $N_G(H)$
contains no copies of $K_{23}$, it follows that $X$ must be either $h_{S}$ or $h_{Sk(d+1)}$. 
Once this is established, the proof proceeds exactly as in the proof of Theorem \ref{gridlemma} without change.

The proof of necessity for $d=2$ is elementary and left to the reader.

condition (2) never applies, since $G$ can have no subgraphs isomorphic to $Q_3$ . Hence condition (1) is satisfied at every $h_0$ and the result follows.

label: natcycles
title: Theorem
body_md:
{\rm (Existence of Natural 2-Cycles)}\label{natcycles}
Suppose that $G_K$ is derived from a simple quadrangulation $K$ of $S^2$.
 Let  $V(G_K) = K_0$ and $ E(G_K) = K_1$, and let $C_n(G_K)$ denote the $Z$-module spanned by singular cubes $\sigma: I_1^n \to G_K$. Then, if $Z = \sum_{i=1}^m \alpha_i z_i$  is a $2$-cycle in $K$ ($\alpha_i \in \mathbb{Z},z_i \in K_2, \partial Z = 0$),
there exists a cycle $\tilde{Z} = \sum_{i=1}^m \alpha_i\tilde{z}_i$ in $C_2(G_K)$ such that for each $i$, $\tilde{z}_i$ is a singular $2$-cube with support equal to the set of vertices of $z_i$.

label: natquests
title: {Problem}
body_md:
\label{natquests}
For $d>2$, define a cubulation $K$ of $S^d$ to be {\em simple} if the $1$-skeleton of every $d$-cell is isomorphic to $Q_d$. 
Then:
\begin{enumerate} \item For which simple cubulations of $S^d$, is every rigid $d$-cube in $G_K$ monophobic?
\item For a simple cubulation of $S^d$, is there always a cycle in $C_d(G_K)$ in which every cell is represented by a singular $d$-cube
with coefficient $\pm 1$?  
\item
Under what conditions does a simple cubulation of $S^d$ have a cycle with all coefficients $+1$?
\end{enumerate}
